articles.title: Durbar legacy in Balochistan
articles.content: THE idea of a durbar still fascinates us and connects us to the subcontinent’s past when kings, rajas, maharajas and nawabs held court. The media, mythology, poetry, theatre, books, and cinema have helped shape the popular image of a ruler seated on his throne, with his ministers and courtiers standing before him. Matters of revenue, war, peace and justice were decided in the ruler’s court. Sometimes, the ruler decided on matters of life and death. However, our fascination may fade once we realise that the legacy of the durbar continues under different names. Pakistan is not the only country carrying this legacy. Many Western countries, including our former colonial ruler, Britain, still retain their monarchies though stripping them of their powers. During the colonial period, the British not only preserved but also strengthened the durbars to control the population and govern indirectly. At the end of British rule, the subcontinent contained approximately 565 princely states. However, historical estimates vary depending on how smaller states are classified. Thirteen were eventually incorporated into Pakistan after their rulers signed Instruments of Accession. Among the courts inherited by Pakistan, none carried greater political symbolism in Balochistan than the Sibi Durbar. It is associated with bitter memories from both the colonial and postcolonial periods. The Sibi Durbar became a major instrument of colonial administrator Robert Sandeman’s frontier policy in the late 19th century. It was an annual winter assembly at which British officials met the officially approved Baloch, Brahui, and Pakhtun chiefs. Tribal disputes were heard, successions and political relationships were considered, honours and allowances were distributed, and the hierarchy created by colonial rule was publicly displayed. Dismantling an institution isn’t the same as changing the political culture that sustained it. Many stories were subsequently associated with the durbar and the British treatment of Baloch and Pakhtun chiefs. One account concerns an earlier Mir Khair Bakhsh Marri, who reportedly refused an order that required the assembled sardars to pull the British political agent’s carriage. According to later accounts, he was punished by being denied privileges granted to more cooperative chiefs. The episode remains part of Baloch political memory. The formal arrangement of the durbar preserved the appearance of the older political order. The chiefs of Sarawan and Jhalawan traditionally sat to the right and left of the Khan of Kalat. Yet the most powerful person in the assembly was not necessarily the Khan. Effective authority rested with the British political agent. Pakistan retained the Sibi Durbar after independence. On Feb 14, 1948, the Quaid addressed what he described as the first “shahi durbar” of Balochistan held under the authority of Pakistan. Speaking to members of the shahi jirga, the sardars and other representatives, he promised political reform. He announced a governor-general’s advisory council as an interim arrangement until a representative constitutional system could be established. One of the last politically consequential Sibi Durbar assemblies took place on Feb 16, 1954. Several sardars submitted a petition to the office of the agent to the governor-general calling for the Balochistan States Union (BSU) to be merged with the former Chief Commissioner’s Province of Balochistan. The BSU emerged from an agreement among the rulers of Kalat, Kharan, Makran, and Lasbela in 1952 and formally came into existence on Oct 3 that year. The four rulers retained limited authority within a union headed initially by the Khan of Kalat. The arrangement, however, survived for only three years. In October 1955, the Union was dissolved and incorporated into the newly created province of West Pakistan under the One Unit scheme. Historians have questioned whether the petition presented at the 1954 durbar represented a spontaneous demand by the sardars or reflected a political process already being encouraged by the central government. Whatever its origins, the episode demonstrated that the durbar could still be used to provide traditional legitimacy for decisions being shaped elsewhere. The abolition of the BSU and the imposition of One Unit deepened political resentment in Balochistan. A few accounts also linked Nawab Nauroz Khan’s uprising with the decision, though his armed struggle began a few years later. The Victoria Memorial Hall, now commonly known as the Jirga Hall, was the principal setting for the Sibi Durbar. It has since been converted into the Sibi Jirga Hall Museum, although it continues to be used for official and cultural functions. Its collection includes photographs, documents, and objects related to the colonial period and the region’s history. Photographs of Jinnah’s 1948 visit preserve the moment when the new state addressed Balochistan through a political institution inherited from the Raj. It is understandable that a newly created country confronting immense administrative and security challenges, could not dismantle every princely and colonial structure overnight. Pakistan required several years, and in some cases decades, to integrate the former princely states. But dismantling an institution is not the same as changing the political culture that sustained it. The princely courts disappeared, the colonial officers departed, and the old administrative structures were formally replaced. Yet the concentration of authority, reliance on selected intermediaries, and preference for managed consultation over genuine representation continued to shape relations between the centre and Balochistan. There is an element of the colonial legacy in Balochistan’s governance model and in the administration of its resources and politics. The Baloch sardars, despite the abolition of the sardari system in 1976, follow the same order and remain subservient to the power elites; hardly anyone raises a voice, and the reason is obvious: they don’t want to lose power or diminish their relationship with the power elites. Though few satirically associate a new institutional mechanism, called ‘workshop’, with the tradition of the durbar, Balochistan is still suffering. Power elites address their grievances through colonial instruments and have not made an earnest attempt to initiate the nation-building process or remove intermediaries — such as sardars and other cronies — between the state and the masses. Perhaps the power elites know that such a shift would change the entire power dynamic in the province and the country.
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: Credentials and character
articles.content: HINA Javed was 45 years old and had been married for nine months when she was found dead in the washroom of her home in Rawalpindi, her hands tied behind her back. According to the FIR filed by her brother, her husband, father-in-law and a domestic worker were accused of her murder. Her brother also alleged that Hina had been subjected to severe violence by her spouse. Every time a case like this breaks, the same reflex follows: shock that the accused was “educated”, a professor no less, someone who had presumably spent years reading, teaching and working at one of the country’s top institutions. The implication is always the same: surely a man like this should have known better. Surely more schooling, more literacy and more exposure to modern ideas would have made him less likely to be violent. It is time we retired that assumption. It is not just simplistic; it can distract us from the work that actually needs to be done. A degree, on its own, does not teach a man to see a woman as his equal. Pakistani research paints a more complicated picture than the comforting assumption that education protects women from violence. A recent analysis of the Pakistan Demographic and Health Survey found that while both women’s and husbands’ education appeared associated with intimate partner violence at one stage of the analysis, neither remained independently significant after other factors were taken into account. Instead, factors such as marital control, knowledge of parental violence and a husband’s use of alcohol were among those significantly associated with intimate partner violence. Education can matter. But it is not a guarantee against abuse. A man can spend 16 years in formal education, earn a doctorate and lecture at a prestigious university, and still carry into his marriage beliefs about entitlement, control and women’s autonomy that education alone has never challenged. Violence is not simply an intellectual deficiency. Information alone does not dismantle it. It is often rooted in a moral and emotional architecture shaped long before university: by ideas about masculinity, anger, entitlement, control and what women are expected to endure. Hina Javed’s case is horrifying, but violence against women in Pakistan is not an aberration. A nationally representative analysis of the 2017-18 Pakistan Demographic and Health Survey found that 33.48 per cent of ever-married women aged 15 to 49 had experienced emotional, physical or sexual violence by a current or most recent husband. Pakistan also ranked last among 148 countries in the World Economic Forum’s 2025 Global Gender Gap Index. These are not the numbers of a society that can afford to assume that educating men is enough. They are the numbers of a society that must think more seriously about how boys are raised, how violence is normalised and how warning signs are ignored. So what does prevention look like, if degrees and professional status are not reliable indicators of safety? It looks like starting decades earlier than a marriage certificate or a professorship: in the home, in early childhood, in the small daily lessons boys absorb about anger, entitlement and control long before anyone calls it ‘gender education’. A boy learns what is acceptable in his treatment of women by observing the relationships around him, by noticing whether his sisters’ opinions carry weight at the dinner table, and by seeing whether other men are ever held accountable when they cross a line. Much of this is not taught in a lecture hall. It is taught, or mistaught, in the ordinary texture of childhood. This means the intervention has to move upstream: into parenting, into how schools respond to boys’ behaviour towards girls from an early age, and into the media and other social institutions that shape ideas of masculinity. It also means taking reports of abuse seriously before violence becomes fatal. The larger problem extends beyond this one case. Violence within a marriage is often treated as a private matter until it becomes impossible to ignore. By then, it may be too late. None of this is an argument against educating men. Education remains valuable for a hundred reasons. But we need to stop confusing credentials with character. A degree tells us what someone has studied, not how he treats his wife. A profession can establish expertise, but it cannot establish emotional maturity, respect for another person’s autonomy or freedom from violent behaviour. Yet we routinely confuse credentials with character. We look at a man’s degree, profession, salary and family background and allow these markers of respectability to stand in for something they cannot establish. Respectability becomes a shorthand for safety. Hina Javed deserved better than a society that waits until a woman is found dead before asking whether there were signs that something was wrong. Preventing the next such death does not start in a university classroom. It starts much earlier: in a nursery, at a dinner table and in the way boys watch the men around them treat women. Degrees can open doors. They can create opportunities. They can produce doctors, lawyers, professors and professionals. But a degree, on its own, does not teach a man to see a woman as his equal. And until we stop mistaking education for decency, we will keep being shocked by violence we should have learned to recognise long before it becomes a headline. The writer is a lawyer and an LLM candidate at Lums.
articles.author: Amber Qayyum

articles.title: Something past fury
articles.content: I HAVE been watching an American television show called Furious. It is about two women on opposite sides of the law. One is a former police officer named Alice who reported her violent boyfriend to their department. The department turned on her, not him. The other is a woman named Catherine who kills men. Men with money, men with records, men with connections that kept them untouchable. The show does not ask you to approve of Catherine. It asks you to notice that by the time she picked up the needle, every system that should have intervened had already left the room. It is remarkably good television. The writer clearly understands something that most crime dramas do not. It’s not who did it; it is what happened before. What trail existed? Who saw it? Who could have stopped it? And why the answer to that last question is almost always nobody, or nobody who mattered. There is a scene in which an older sex crimes detective, Nora, delivers a monologue by a hospital bed about what years of watching children abused has done to her. “You think you’re ever going to catch anyone who matters?” she says. Name, hashtag, outrage, silence, name. The loop does not break. I was watching this when I read about Hina Javed. Hina was married for nine months. She was found in a bathroom in Rawalpindi with her hands tied behind her back and a cloth over her mouth. Suspects were arrested. But as with so many cases, the questions that followed were not just about what happened in that bathroom. They were about what was known before, and what was not acted on. I should have felt outrage. I felt recognition. This is what is left after years of hashtags and celebrity Instagram stories and tagging chief ministers in posts that ask them to act “not as a politician, but as a woman”. The outrage cycle is so familiar now that I can map it before it begins. A woman dies. A name trends. Celebrities share the family’s letter. Someone tags Maryam Nawaz. An Instagram justice page gains 3,000 followers. Then we move on, until the next name. I referred to my 2020 column about women’s anger. I had quoted Rebecca Traister, who argued that anger has connective power, that it can be channelled into structural change. I had also quoted Brittney Cooper, who wrote that the quickest way to discredit a woman is to call her angry. I believed then that something was shifting. Women journalists had signed a petition against online harassment. Aurat March was growing. Women were organising. Six years later, I am not sure what was built. The petition did not produce a mechanism. The march still happens and still meets the same resistance. Online abuse of women journalists is worse, not better. And another woman was found dead in a bathroom with her hands tied. The show is called Furious. I am something past furious. The numbness is not indifference. It is the thing that happens when you have watched the same sequence enough times to know where it ends. Name, hashtag, outrage, silence, name. The loop does not break because it was never designed to. In the show, Catherine kills because she concluded that nothing else was on offer. Alice stays inside the system and is punished for it. Nora stays and is hollowed out by it. Three women, three responses to the same failure. None of them produces safety. The show is honest enough to say so. In Pakistan, we have a fourth response. We post. We share. We tag. We write columns. I am writing one now. I know it will not save the next Hina. I know that the next case will also have a trail that should have mattered, and that the outrage when it surfaces will also be sincere and also be useless. Not fury. We have had fury. What we have never had is a system that treats a harassment complaint at the workplace as information that matters beyond that workplace. We have never had a mechanism that connects a pattern of complaints to a warning before a marriage. We have never had a bureaucracy that treats violence against women as a problem to be solved with procedure rather than a tragedy to be responded to with speeches. Nora’s line keeps coming back to me. You think you’re ever going to catch anyone who matters? In Pakistan the question is simpler. You think you’re ever going to stop anyone before it matters? I will finish the show. I expect it will not answer the question either. That is the difference between good fiction and bad reality. Fiction is allowed to leave the question open. Reality is not supposed to, but does. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: India’s relevance?
articles.content: INDIA is the most populous country in the world. With a nominal GDP of $4.15 trillion, it is the sixth-largest economy globally, with a big market share that makes countries want to do business with it. Its expansive territory extends down to the northern tip of the Indian Ocean. Despite this strategic weight, why is India losing proportionate relevance in today’s global geopolitics? Five reasons can be identified. Firstly, for decades, India was a partner of choice for the US in countering China’s rise. Imagining itself as the net security provider for South Asia, India joined the America-led Indo-Pacific Strategy, Quad, I2U2, and IMEC. Beijing sensed well in time that America was encircling China with the help of India, Japan and Australia. It could also see that America continued to stir trouble in the South China Sea and could well choke Chinese exports passing through the Pacific and Indian oceans. Pursuant to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Greater Eurasia partnership initiative, China is increasingly using three overland northern routes and one sea route through the Arctic Ocean. Adapting quickly, America decided to work with China for “constructive strategic stability”. This was announced during President Donald Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping in May 2026. The US also reverted its Indo-Pacific Command back to Pacific Command. India’s salience began to change from a strategic US partner to a commercially relevant country. Secondly, nothing has altered the balance of power in South Asia more profoundly than theevents of May 2025. Encouraged by its blatant aggression against Pakistan in 2016 and 2019, Narendra Modi’s government launched missile strikes against nine targets in Pakistan on May 7, wrongly assuming that Pakistan would not be able to respond. It learned to its surprise that Pakistan not only responded robustly on May 10 but also forced India to seek a ceasefire through the US leadership. When the US president helped secure a ceasefire, India did not have the grace to accept the role the US had played. As a result, it found itself in an uncomfortable situation in which the country it sought to please was unresponsive. Pakistan’s military credentials, on the other hand, were recognised by the world at large. Soon after the confrontation, Saudi Arabia entered into aStrategic Mutual Defence Agreementwith Pakistan in September 2025. Earlier this month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye signed theMakkah Joint Defence Agreement, making India wonder how and why it lost its strategic space in West Asia. Thirdly, South Asia is the world’s least integrated region. A major factor is that India has unfriendly ties with most of its neighbours. It has also made Saarc dysfunctional lest other South Asian states team up to counterbalance it. Indian policymakers have failed to recognise that India’s global stature and relevance will never be realised unless it can take regional countries along. The May 2025 conflict has altered the balance of power in South Asia. Fourthly, for some time, India has tried to project itself as a champion of the Global South. The reality is that China is miles ahead in cultivating developing countries through massive investment in infrastructure, energy and other projects. Furthermore, India has sought to lean closer to the US, clearly signalling its priorities to the Global South. For instance, India opposed the creation of a common BRICS currency to challenge the US dollar, though it does not reject bilateral trade in national currencies. Finally, it was Pakistan, and not India, that was deemed a crediblemediatorto bring about a ceasefire to the 40-day war between the US and Iran. Pakistan hosted the US and Iran in Islamabad for direct talks, helped conclude the Islamabad MoU, and is continuing its efforts to achieve peace in West Asia. Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts have been appreciated by the entire world except India and Israel that have been courting each other. Three days before the US-Iran war started, the Indian prime ministerwas in Israelpraising the latter as the fatherland without saying a word about the Israeli genocide in Gaza. India’s real priorities stood exposed to Iran and the Gulf countries. Importantly, Pakistan’s rising diplomatic profile has also thwarted India’s decade-long effort to isolate it. While these five reasons have made India strategically less relevant today, Pakistan’s diplomatic and military profile has continued to rise. For Pakistan to sustain its global relevance, an equal effort is needed to build up its economic profile. Given the close linkages between a country’s citizen-centric governance and economic output, the recent debate over how to devolve resources to the grassroots is timely. It should be taken to its logical conclusion. The writer is the chairman of Sanober Institute and a former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
articles.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry

articles.title: Steep challenge
articles.content: AN abundance of good fortune has landed a 46-year-old barrister, Syed Iftikhar Ali Gillani, in the hot seat. He will serve as the 17th prime minister of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, having beenelectedto the post on Friday with 30 votes from his party, the PML-N. For now, Mr Gillani heads an incomplete legislative assembly, with seven seats representing the Poonch and Sudhnoti districtsyet to be filleddue to the law-and-order situation in those areas. He made note of that fact in his inaugural speech, hoping that the remainder of the electoral process will be completed soon. He also promised employment, especially for the youth, recruitment on merit, transparency and anti-corruption measures, improvement in education and healthcare, digitising the economy, and launching a portal to address citizens’ grievances. That makes for a bold, positive start to what is bound to be a challenging assignment. Mr Gillani will remain under constant scrutiny, including from his own party. The recent general election in AJK has remained marred by controversy. There were frequent and vociferousaccusations of impropriety and alleged rigging, including from one of the PML-N’s most important allies at the centre. The AJK Election Commission, too, controversially decided it would declare voting results after each phase of the election, raising serious questions regarding electoral propriety. And then there were the large-scale and often violent protests that disrupted the process, which have yet to be conclusively addressed. To top it off, Mr Gillani’s candidature for the premiership also drew strong resistance from within his own party. Senior PML-N figures, including the AJK chapter president Shah Ghulam Qadir and former AJK prime minister Raja Farooq Haider, openly and strongly opposed his nomination. Mr Qadir had been considered the leading contender before Mr Gillani’s entry, but the party seems to have had other plans. Critics also pointed to the fact that Mr Gillani lost the Muzaffarabad-III constituency he had contested in the general election and was only returned to the AJK Legislative Assembly on a reserved technocrat seat. This clashed with the PML-N’s own position on ‘respecting the vote’, as the critics pointed out. Still, it appears that the party’s central leadership insisted on a younger face over the old guard in AJK. Whether that bet pays off remains to be seen. Mr Gillani will need to prove his doubters wrong while placating those elements in AJK that resisted or boycotted the electoral process. The latter may be the most sensitive aspect of his job, given the criticality of restoring stability in the region. He has been involved in AJK politics at least since 2010, and has previously served in the AJK cabinet. Whether or not those experiences have prepared him adequately for the premiership will soon become evident.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: The missing
articles.content: PAKISTAN has for decades grappled with the problem of missing persons, as powerful actors within the state have been accused of tolerating the practice of enforced disappearances. Due to the sustained activism of those whose loved ones have reportedly been ‘disappeared’, as well as rights groups, the state has at least acknowledged that the problem exists, and formed official bodies to look into the matter. But today, as the world observes the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, the state must pledge to eliminate this unlawful practice and handle suspects within constitutional bounds. At least two bodies have been set up at the federal level, with the Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances primarily looking into cases, while a provincial committee formed by the Balochistan High Court is also in operation. Balochistan and KP face the highest number of missing persons, though cases have been reported from other provinces as well. According to the COIED, 8,873 cases were “disposed of” between March 2011, when the commission was formed, and August 2025. Yet independent observers, such as HRCP, say these figures are “vastly underreported”. Moreover, last year the Balochistan Assembly amended the provincial antiterrorism law allowing for detention without charge for up to three months. This can hardly be called a progressive step towards bringing transparency to the issue of missing persons. There is no doubt that the state continues to face critical law and order challenges, such as insurgencies and terrorism. But these difficulties cannot be tackled by skirting constitutional rights, and creating parallel systems that are beyond public scrutiny. Arguably, when officialdom hauls people away without due process, and without telling their families why and where they are being held, it only adds to the people’s alienation from the state. A confident state relies on the law to prosecute those it believes are involved in wrongdoing. Or if the rulers believe the legal system is broken, they should correct it without compromising fundamental rights. A weak legal system is no excuse for violating rights. If the state believes individuals are involved in wrongdoing, instead of keeping them incommunicado, it must produce them before a court, so that they can defend themselves.
articles.author: Editorial
